body_markdown:
What a run the Mark Series had. Such memorable cars, such decadent luxury. And my grandfather, Bob Klockau, was fond of them. He had three over the years, so I’ve always loved them too. Way back when I was a little kid, my folks got me a Tomica/Pocket Cars Continental Mark IV in 1/64 scale. It was blue with a white top. It survived, and now sits among a ton of other scale Lincoln models today. So when I unexpectedly spot one, I get *extremely* excited.


On the first Saturday of June, I met my friend Jessica Grissom and a few of her friends to check out the Rhubarb Fest in Aledo, Illinois. I’d never gone, and thought it might be fun. Some of you regular readers may be shocked to learn that a car show was not part of the activities, yet your author still willingly went. And had fun despite getting a slightly sunburned face. Yet, as it all too often happens, a classic car found me.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


I was almost back to town from Aledo, driving through Milan, IL, when I spotted a familiar Parthenon grill grinning back at me from a side street. After almost crashing the car, I recovered and drove around the block, pulled astride with the Caddy, hit the hazard lights, and leaped out of the car.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Initially I thought it was a ’75, as it had the gorgeous deep-dish polished aluminum wheels, and those did not appear until the 1975 model year. But it had a full vinyl roof, not the Landau roof.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


One look at the steering wheel and I knew it had to be a 1974, as it had the two spokes at 9 and 3 o’clock. Starting in 1975 it was redesigned, still with two spokes, but they were turned downward, approximately in the 4 and 8 o’clock positions.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


It was also incredibly, incredibly nice. The interior was like new, as was the paint, trim, and well, everything else. And it even had the power glass moonroof! This car was LOADED.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Keep in mind the Continental Mark IV was the flagship. The top of the line, a personal luxury coupe with every extra you could possibly want. And even a “standard” Mark IV was a very, very nice car. And it should have been, with a base MSRP of $10,194. For comparison’s sake, in 1974 a new Ford Maverick went for $3025.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


On top of that were the Luxury Groups. In 1973, the first version was the Silver Luxury Group. It was available with or without a power glass moonroof, and the interior featured cranberry Victoria velour, with cranberry leather optional.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


In 1974, there was also a new Gold Luxury Group, but the Silver Luxury Group was still available. It was a $400 option, or $777.40 if you selected the group with the power glass moonroof.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As the large, plush 1974 Continental brochure stated, “Adding luxury to luxury. To all of the standard luxuries of the Continental Mark IV, add silver. Silver Moondust metallic paint outside. A choice of remarkable embellishments inside: High-lustre silver leather seating surfaces with silver door panels and carpeting.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“Or red leather seating surfaces and red door panels and carpeting. Or cranberry Media velour upholstery with cranberry door panels and carpeting. All have twenty-five ounce color-keyed cut-pile carpeting throughout the interior and in the luggage compartment.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“The silver Levant grain vinyl roof is standard. The silver glass Moonroof is optional. It has a one-way glass roof you can see through, while your privacy is maintained.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“The silver Continental Mark IV has become one of the most desired choices of America’s unique personal luxury car.” And it was a *solid* personal luxury car, with a curb weight of 5362 pounds. While I don’t have the breakout for Luxury Group production, a total of 57,316 Mark IVs were built for 1974.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


But as interesting as all that is, what *really* got me excited was the dealer tag on today’s featured Nimitz-class luxocruiser: Bob Neal Lincoln-Mercury.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


You see, this was the dealership where my grandparents bought their Lincolns and T-Birds for many years. My often-mentioned grandfather’s first Lincoln, a green ’66 Continental sedan, came from here, as did the triple dark green 1969 Mark III, triple dark green ’72 Mark IV and triple navy blue ’77 Mark V.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


This was the dealership where my uncle Dave tried to talk my grandma Ruby into buying a brand-new, yellow 1971 DeTomaso Pantera. I recently asked my dad about this episode, and he said she was actually receptive to it, but my grandfather apparently intervened and she kept her Thunderbird. My other uncle, Don Symmonds, was a master mechanic there. My grandparents always made sure he was the one assigned to work on their cars.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


My uncle Dave, a teenager at the time, was a lot jockey there too, around the time this Mark IV came off the truck in Rock Island. The day after I saw this car, I texted him pics of the car and the Bob Neal tag.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


He responded, “Holy crap! I might have driven that one. The Lincoln building was built for much smaller cars, and jockeying those mothers around would be like docking the Queen Mary at Sunset Marina!”


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The Mark IV continued for 1975 and 1976, and for 1977 the basic chassis was given a sharper, more creased body and became the Mark V. Starting in ’75, many more Luxury Groups were added, including Saddle and White, Lipstick (a combination of white and bold red), Jade, and others.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As for Bob Neal Ford and Bob Neal Lincoln-Mercury, my grandfather and Dick McCarthy (a partner in my grandfather’s law firm and long-time friend of our family) actually helped get the business started and were investors in it. But old Bob Neal (he was famous for his TV commercials on the local stations: he’d always pose next to a weathered car, tout the low price, and say, “and it’s got a rrrrrradio!”) evidently pulled a kind of[Jerry Lundegaard-esque](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0116282/characters/nm0000513/) flim flam: He’d sell new cars, but “forget” to send the titles to owners, so it looked like he had more assets than he really did.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Legend has it that one day, he parked in his driveway, went into his house, and sometime between then and the next morning, fled the metro area. We later heard he went out to Arizona. No one in the Quad Cities ever saw him in the area again, to my knowledge. What had been Bob Neal Ford/Lincoln-Mercury later became Erv Peters Ford, and my uncle Don continued to work for that entity for several years. Much, much later it became Wakeen’s, a Sea Ray boat dealership. Kind of appropriate since the same address had sold giant luxury land yachts years earlier!


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Around 2007 or so, I was in Dick McCarthy’s office with John Gianulis (another long-time family friend; he worked down the block from Dick’s law firm), and I mentioned Bob Neal. John thought he was still alive and living in Phoenix. And that was the last new info on the whole debacle I ever received. Both John and Dick are gone now too. They were good guys, treated awkward 20-something me as an equal, and I remember many times we went to lunch and would hear stories about stuff that happened in town in 1955 or 1971 or 1983. I miss them.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Seeing this Mark brought all those memories back, and for that, I thank the owner of this car who rolled it out on his lawn one nice late-spring Saturday. It’s not always about the cars: it’s about the memories associated with cars and the loved ones we remember.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And that’s why I write.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)
